newsitem.title: USA: Bout with cancer radicalized flight attendant.
newsitem.headline: Bout with cancer radicalized flight attendant.

text.p: Norma Broin, who has worked as a flight attendant most of her life, remembers the days when aircraft ventilation systems became so overwhelmed with cigarette smoke that the air would turn blue.
"Those gas-permeable contact lenses, oh yeah, they turned yellow. Your eyes would sting, you'd have headaches, your chest would burn," she said in an interview.
"You would ask the captain to turn the 'No Smoking' sign on for a while so that people would stop smoking. We would actually go up in the cockpit and use some of the pilot's oxygen," she said.

But it took a bout of lung cancer to make Broin, a political conservative and lifetime non-smoker, angry enough to mount a legal challenge against the cigarette companies she considers responsible for those working conditions -- and for her disease.

That legal challenge will go to court next week as Broin vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. et al -- a $5 billion class-action suit that claims damages on behalf of some 60,000 non-smoking airline flight attendants who allegedly contracted lung diseases and other ailments from secondhand smoke on U.S. passenger jets.
The landmark suit will be the first class-action and the first secondhand smoke suit against tobacco companies to go to trial when it opens in a Miami courtroom on June 2.

"For me, this just boils down to what's right and what's wrong. It's not right to do something that costs people their lives," Broin said. "And ... if you want to go by statistics, when people have lung cancer, fewer than 7 percent of those people are alive seven years later to talk about it."
Broin, a mother of two children who is married to a U.S. Marine, found out she had a particularly aggressive form of lung cancer in 1989, when she was just 34.

Though she was able to beat the odds through surgery and luck -- her cancer was discovered early because doctors were trying to explain unrelated chest pains and tingling in her arms -- the disease confounded her.

Not only a non-smoker, Broin is an active member of the Mormon church, which forbids smoking. Because her social life centres around her church, she had rarely been around cigarettes and other tobacco products, except during hours spent serving peanuts and cocktails while working on jetliners.
"I really didn't, other than in my work environment, have a huge amount of exposure to cigarette smoke," she said.
After her diagnosis, surgery and recovery, Broin researched lung disease and cigarette smoke and became angrier and angrier.
Along the way, Broin, now 42, missed years of working and had to contend with the fears of her children, now 15 and 13. She even missed her son's first day of kindergarten.

"It was like, should I do it, shouldn't I do it? There was no way I couldn't ... It was just festering, it had to be done. If you know something is not right, you know you have a responsibility," she said from her home in Stafford, Va.
Finally, she searched for a lawyer who would take her case -- at a time when cigarette makers had never lost a liability suit.
She found Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt, a husband-and-wife law team in Miami Beach.
"Without her, there wouldn't be a flight attendants' case," Stanley Rosenblatt said.

"She became a student of the whole thing. She talked to her doctor. She talked to public health officials. She was absolutely convinced that her lung cancer was caused by secondhand smoke. And she talked to her co-workers and discovered they were getting sick, too."

Broin, who has returned to flying -- now in smoke-free airliners -- said she expected she would be called to testify in her landmark case, and confessed she did not relish the thought, just as she does not enjoy her frequent contacts with the media.
"I call them Pepto-Bismol days," she said, in a reference to the popular medicine often used for upset stomachs.
"Certainly, I suspect the hard part is yet to come. For the last seven or so years that I've been doing this, it's been educating and time-demanding, emotionally demanding, physically demanding.
"The tobacco companies, when we go to trial, will slander me in every possible way," she said. "I think I would have rather just lived a nice life, raised my family."
